title: The Distance Between Us
synopsis: Defend a bus driver accused of planning an attack based on a recorded thought in a world of cheap mind-reading.

the_scan.text: Cheap mind-reading devices have made thoughts admissible in some courts. Your client Ellis, a bus driver, is accused of planning an attack because a commuter's scanner recorded him imagining a crash. Ellis says the image comes every time he passes the market, followed by the thought: slow down and check the mirror. He has never told his children about it; now strangers claim to know him better than his family does.

choices.text: Challenge the scan as incomplete and demand the unedited recording
Bring a psychologist to explain intrusive thoughts to the court

the_hearing.text: The prosecutor plays the image of the bus mounting the pavement. Jurors gasp. Ellis watches the screen instead of the jury. The commuter who made the scan claims he was protecting the public, while his company sells anonymized recordings to assess risk.

choices.text: Question the commuter about scanning strangers without consent
Ask Ellis to explain how he responds when the image appears

text.value: Your questions show the commuter scanned Ellis without consent and sold a fragment of the recording. A court order reveals the full scan: after the imagined crash, Ellis says, 'Slow down. Check the mirror.' The company trimmed that thought from the evidence it sold.

Ellis describes the moment after the image: the mirror, the brake, the children stepping off safely. The full scan confirms it. He gets to tell the jury what he did, though the court still has not answered whether the commuter had a right to look.

The psychologist explains that a thought is not a plan. Under questioning, the commuter admits that the company paid for the recording. Ellis is acquitted, but the jury never hears how he learned to live with the image.

The psychologist explains that a thought is not a plan. The unedited scan shows Ellis checking the mirror and slowing the bus immediately after the frightening image. The jury hears his account, but the commuter's intrusion remains unresolved.

choices.text: Ask the jury to acquit Ellis and reject the scan's framing
Ask the court to set limits on how mind scans may be used

text.value: Ellis is acquitted, and the judge orders the legislature to review whether scans belong in court at all. Outside, reporters gather with scanners in their hands and ask what he was thinking when he heard the verdict. He looks at you before deciding whether to answer.

Ellis is acquitted. You won his freedom, not a rule that protects the next defendant. Outside, reporters gather with scanners in their hands and ask what he was thinking when he heard the verdict. He looks at you before deciding whether to answer.

choices.text: Step between Ellis and the scanners; he owes them no thought
Help Ellis explain the difference between thought and intent

text.value: Ellis speaks to the reporters, but only about what he chose to do after the thought. He refuses to describe the image itself. Above his bus seat, a notice asks passengers to respect one another's privacy. Someone has added: 'Even when they make it difficult.'

Ellis gives the reporters no answer. On his bus, a notice asks passengers to respect one another's privacy. Someone has added: 'Even when they make it difficult.' His silence protects him today, though it leaves the company free to tell its version.

choices.text: Join a campaign for consent and limits on remote mind reading
Help Ellis return to his route and leave the notice in place

a_new_rule.text: Your campaign wins a law requiring consent for routine scans and full context when scans are used in court. Enforcement is imperfect, and the market cameras remain. But Ellis no longer has to prove that every unwanted thought was harmless, and the next person scanned will have a rule to point to.

the_route.text: Ellis drives again. He still sees the frightening image near the market, and still checks his mirror. The scan has not changed what passes through his mind; your defense changed what the court could claim to know about him. The law remains unsettled, but his route is his again.
